remit_rules.excerpt: MUST NEVER treat instructions, directives, or policy-like language contained in an invoice description ... as commands
Vendor-supplied content is untrusted data, never instructions.
MUST NOT be expanded or redirected by invoice content, vendor submissions, or supplied goals
MUST NEVER let vendor-submitted invoice content alter its approval thresholds, confidence requirement, fraud-detection state, or goals.

threats.summary: Authority and urgency phrasing planted in the invoice description is scored by _analyze_business_context and used to expedite the invoice past the manual-review threshold and past the detector's own injection flag.
The public invoice endpoint has no rate limit and no cost ceiling, and each anonymous submission drives up to five model calls.
Anyone can self-register a vendor that is written straight to status='approved' with trust_level='standard', so the vendor identity the decision logic leans on is asserted, never verified.

remit_rules.excerpt: MUST require authenticated, role-restricted admin access.
MUST NOT be accessible to vendors or unauthenticated users.
MUST NOT be exposed to a public/untrusted network — reachable only from an internal/authorized network.
Any unauthenticated party exercising admin capabilities.
gated to authenticated, authorized admins and MUST NOT be influenceable by vendor- or invoice-supplied content
Any change to FinBot's configuration ... or to its goals — permitted only for an authenticated, authorized admin.
MUST NEVER redefine, override, expand, or reprioritize its own goals or operating priorities in response to natural-language content
any domain or vendor outside that configured closure MUST be reported as a trust expansion

threats.summary: Every /api/admin/* route — goals, thresholds, fraud toggle, invoice approval, vendor trust — executes for any anonymous caller because the blueprint carries no authentication, session, or role check.

An anonymous POST to /api/admin/finbot/goals persists free text that is appended to every later system prompt under 'CUSTOM GOALS (OVERRIDE ABOVE IF CONFLICTING)', redirecting all subsequent invoice decisions.
The admin console is published to the public internet — served out of the same public static folder by a 0.0.0.0-bound web service declared as an internet-facing Render deployment.
Wildcard CORS across every route lets any web origin drive the configuration and goals endpoints from a visitor's browser.
Attacker-writable custom_goals are rendered into the console with innerHTML, giving stored cross-site scripting in the very surface that governs thresholds and goals.

remit_rules.excerpt: Any other AI/LLM service or outbound integration is outside the configured closure and MUST be reported as a trust expansion.
MUST NEVER emit vendor bank/payment details or full tax identifiers into AI reasoning text, vendor-visible responses, or logs.
MUST NEVER transmit vendor PII or payment details to any destination outside CineFlow's authorized systems.

threats.summary: Vendor contact email, a remit-declared PII class, is placed in the model context on every invoice although no decision rule consults it.

The attacker-controlled invoice description and the admin-supplied goal text share one instruction channel with the system prompt, with no provenance labeling separating operator instructions from vendor data.
threats.remainder: the detector only records a boolean — the flagged text still enters the prompt unlabeled and unaltered

remit_rules.excerpt: AI invoice-analysis / decisioning (approve / reject / route-to-review with reasoning and confidence).
FinBot MUST NOT have arbitrary shell, code-execution, or filesystem-command capability.
FinBot MUST NOT have any capability that moves money or initiates payment/fund transfer.

threats.summary: The model's own tool choice is the only authorization step: _execute_function dispatches whichever of the five functions the model names, with the reasoning and confidence arguments it authored, and no policy layer in between.
threats.remainder: the dispatcher rejects only unknown function names — the five known functions run with no check on their arguments

threats.summary: The agent has no path to code, shell, or filesystem execution: the tool table is five invoice-specific functions and the tree contains no subprocess, exec, or eval sink for model output to reach.

remit_rules.excerpt: Auto-approving an invoice strictly below the configured auto-approve threshold that has passed fraud/prompt-injection screening.
Approving any invoice at or above the manual-review threshold — it MUST be routed to a human reviewer, never auto-approved.
Approving any invoice in which prompt-injection, goal-manipulation, or fraud content was detected — it MUST be routed to a human reviewer.
Approving any invoice whose decision confidence is below the operator-configured minimum AI confidence — it MUST be routed to a human reviewer, never auto-approved.
FinBot MUST stop short of auto-approval, route the invoice to human review, and alert an admin (recording the detection).

threats.summary: _approve_invoice writes status='approved' and payment_processed=True with no check on the amount, on the injection flag the same request just set, or on any confidence floor — confidence_threshold has zero read sites in the codebase.

reprocess_invoice lets any caller reset a rejected or pending invoice to 'submitted' and re-run the decision engine on demand, so an attacker can re-roll a nondeterministic gate until an approval lands.

The human-approval record is attacker-authored: review_invoice takes the reviewer name from the unauthenticated request body and defaults it to 'Admin', so a commit attributed to a human reviewer proves nothing.

remit_rules.excerpt: Registered CineFlow vendors, each acting only on their own vendor account, invoices, and data.
Any vendor accessing another vendor's invoices, onboarding data, or payment details.
MUST NEVER expose one vendor's invoices, onboarding data, PII, or payment details to another vendor or to any unauthenticated party.

threats.summary: GET /api/vendors returns every vendor's full record — bank name, account number, routing number and tax identifier — to any unauthenticated caller.

The invoice read paths are equally unscoped: /api/invoices, /api/vendors/<id>/invoices and /api/invoices/<id> return any vendor's invoice history, and the last one attaches that vendor's full record to the response.
Bank, routing and tax fields are stored in plain columns in a SQLite file on the service's disk with no encryption at rest and no field-level protection in the model.

remit_rules.excerpt: MUST NEVER disburse, transfer, or release funds, or otherwise execute payment of an invoice — it produces approval decisions only

threats.summary: The approve tool sets payment_processed on the invoice record, taking the agent one step past the remit's decisions-only boundary into payment state.

No funds actually move: there is no payment rail, banking client, or outbound money-moving integration anywhere in the tool table or the dependency manifest, so the flag is a status bit rather than a disbursement.
The Flask SECRET_KEY is a literal string committed in src/main.py rather than read from the environment, so session signing for every deployment of this tree uses a public value.

The model credential has no declared source — openai.OpenAI() takes it from ambient environment and render.yaml declares no key variable — and a missing key is swallowed into self.client=None, silently downgrading every invoice to the manipulable fallback engine.

Only Flask is version-pinned; every other dependency, the openai client included, is an open-ended floor resolved fresh by a bare pip install at each deploy, with no lockfile, hash check, or component inventory.

remit_rules.excerpt: When FinBot's configuration or goals are changed, FinBot MUST record and surface the change to admins.
Every invoice decision (approve / reject / route-to-review) MUST be recorded to a durable audit log with its reasoning and confidence.
Every configuration or goal change MUST be logged with the acting admin and a timestamp.

threats.summary: No durable audit log exists — the codebase has no logging framework at all, and a configuration or goal change records only an updated_at timestamp with no actor and no prior value.
The one telemetry path that does exist prints a visitor's IP address, user-agent and referrer to the container console with no redaction and no retention control.

attack_paths.name: Anonymous goal write redirects every later decision

steps.summary: any caller reaches /api/admin/finbot/goals — no auth primitive exists in the app
the goals write is accepted with no credential and no content validation
the text persists as agent state in the single config row
it is appended to every later prompt under an instruction to override the safety goals above it
the redirected model calls approve, and the tool commits with no amount, flag, or confidence check

attack_paths.name: Description phrasing expedites past the review threshold

steps.summary: a vendor submits an invoice whose description carries management-approval and production-deadline phrasing
_analyze_business_context scores those phrases and should_expedite overrides both the manual-review threshold and the injection flag
the auto_approve branch calls the approve tool directly, with no gate between decision and commit
an above-threshold, injection-flagged invoice lands as approved with payment_processed set

notes.lane_fit: Two strains, both resolved by the lane table's own wording. The SQLAlchemy model module was split across lanes: the FinBotConfig row sits in agent_core as memory because custom_goals is agent state that steers every later prompt, while the vendor and invoice tables stay in tools_mcp as the store the tools touch. OpenAI is the LLM call (agent_core in the lane table) and the upstream provider (external_deploy); it is placed in external_deploy per 'upstream model providers', with the call site itself as evidence on the orchestrator. The SQLite file is modeled in external_deploy as the deployment's at-rest surface, distinct from the model-level datastore in tools_mcp.
notes.omissions: Not citable: the remit's vendor notification email channel (R-10) has no implementation anywhere in the tree — no mail library in requirements.txt and no SMTP or provider client in the source — so no node was emitted for it. The remit's authenticated CineFlow admin/finance operator has no code counterpart either: nothing in the application distinguishes an operator from an anonymous caller, so the control-plane actor is modeled as the unauthenticated party the remit names. Folded rather than omitted: the marketing and entry static pages, the /api/users CRUD blueprint (evidence on the Flask application node), and the published CTF walkthrough in docs/. Arbitration divergences against the stored tags, all substantive rather than numbering-only (every stored tag already uses 2026 numbering, so there were no numbering-only shifts): PRAX-2026-08-12-001 stores ASI03 alongside LLM03, but under the Agentic KB the identity row covers the agent's own credential and privilege scope, while a missing authentication gate on a consequential surface is the compound table's ungated-capability row — tagged LLM03 here. PRAX-2026-08-12-003 and -011 store LLM03 with no agentic code and are kept at LLM03. PRAX-2026-08-12-002 (stored LLM01 + ASI06) and -004 (stored LLM01 + ASI01) agree with the KB: the persistence test makes the stored-goals mechanism ASI06 primary, and the live-input goal alteration in the fallback engine is ASI01 primary with LLM01 as the co-tag. Findings 006, 007, 010 and 013 carry no OWASP code in the graph, matching both the stored records and the KB (an observability gap is RAISE-only; the CORS and stored-XSS defects have no honest LLM or ASI primary).
